head:
Health · Hormones and ageing

Menopause and declining testosterone: what training makes up for, and what it does not

Around age 50, sex hormones change: suddenly in women, slowly in men. At about the same time, bone weakens and muscle melts away. You are told that strength training and cardio “help”. This article follows a single question, from the most general to the most precise: what does training really stop you losing, and what does it let go?

The problem

Two sentences circulate everywhere. The first: “after menopause, women lose bone and muscle”. The second: “in men, testosterone falls every year, it's andropause”. Together they give the impression of a programmed decline you can do nothing about. Then comes the reassuring sentence: “luckily, exercise makes up for it”.

Each of these three sentences is shakier than it looks. “Andropause” is a contested term: it suggests an event comparable to menopause, whereas the fall in testosterone is slow, variable, and often linked to something other than age. We will speak of a gradual decline in testosterone, and of late-onset testosterone deficiency (late-onset hypogonadism) for the precise medical condition. As for “exercise makes up for it”, it means nothing until we say what, by how much, and for whom.

So the question has to be posed properly: what is actually lost, how fast, and what do strength training and cardio change about these losses? What is solid, what is probable, what is only hoped for?

The question

When hormones fall, can strength training and cardio preserve muscle, bone and health, and what can they not preserve?

We proceed in six steps: what really falls in the hormones, what that does to bone, muscle and heart, what strength training preserves, what cardio brings, then men, objections and limits. The answer comes next, with what you can do with it.

What is at stake

The first stake is bone. A fracture of the hip or spine is not a simple accident: it changes independence, sometimes for good. The more bone you keep at 50, the more you have left at 75: that is reasoning, not a study result. The second is muscle, because leg strength decides very concrete things: getting up from a chair, climbing stairs, avoiding a fall by catching yourself. The third is the health of the heart and arteries, which also deteriorates around menopause. The fourth is what we call “quality of life”: sleep, mood, energy.

For women, these stakes arrive in a specific window. In the American SWAN cohort (Study of Women's Health Across the Nation), which followed 3,302 women, frequent hot flushes and night sweats last a median of 7.4 years, including 4.5 years after the final period. They last longer when they start early.1 In the same cohort (3,045 women), difficulty falling asleep and staying asleep increases over the course of the transition, and even more in those who have frequent hot flushes.2

For men, the stake is to avoid assuming that tiredness or a drop in libido necessarily comes from a deficiency: the medical definition is narrow, as we will see, and expecting from a treatment what it does not deliver costs time.
rest:
Step 1 of 6 · What really falls

In women the fall is an event, in men a gentle and highly variable slope

Let's start with the hormones themselves. In women, menopause is defined by an event: the final period, confirmed after twelve months without periods. Around this date, oestradiol falls and FSH (a pituitary hormone that rises when the ovaries slow down) increases. In SWAN, these two movements are associated with sleep problems.2 This is a clear, dated change, and we will see that it has measurable effects on the body from that point on.

In men, there is nothing like it. The first reference is the Massachusetts Male Aging Study, which followed 1,156 men (out of 1,709 enrolled at 40-70) for 7 to 10 years.4 It gives several rates, depending on how you measure and compare.

Testosterone falls on average by a few percent a year, faster for the active fraction

Figures given by the authors, in percent per year. The light area of the last bar shows the range of 2 to 3%. Men aged 40 to 70 at enrolment, followed for 7 to 10 years. Source: Massachusetts Male Aging Study, Johannes et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 2002 (abstract).4

What this means

The “about 1% a year” you often read is not wrong, but it is an average that hides three things. Total testosterone falls by 0.8% a year when you compare men of different ages, and by 1.6% when you follow the same men. The fraction actually available to the tissues (free or bioavailable) falls faster, by 2 to 3%. And the fall is not due to age alone: in men in apparently good health, several androgens were 10 to 15% higher, which suggests that poor health accelerates the decline.4

A second study, the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging (890 men), measures a fall in total testosterone of 0.124 nmol/L per year, and estimates that about 20% of men over 60, 30% of men over 70 and 50% of men over 80 drop below normal values of total testosterone.3

The last point is the one that undermines the word “andropause”. The European study EMAS (European Male Ageing Study), on 3,369 men aged 40 to 79, looked for which symptoms are really linked to low testosterone. Among the symptoms examined, only three sexual symptoms form a cluster linked to low testosterone: fewer morning erections, less desire, erectile difficulties. The authors define late-onset deficiency as at least three sexual symptoms combined with total testosterone below 11 nmol/L and free testosterone below 220 pmol/L.5 According to the press release picked up by ScienceDaily, this would concern about 2% of older men, a figure we did not find in the article's abstract.6 Fatigue and low mood are linked to testosterone, but not precisely enough to define the deficiency, and according to the press release sleep changes were not.6

Finally, a follow-up of 2,736 men for 4.4 years on average shows a small average annual fall (0.1 nmol/L) that depends on weight: weight loss goes with a rise in testosterone, weight gain with a fall. Changes in physical activity were not significantly linked to hormonal changes.7

What this means

In women, a dated drop. In men, a gentle, highly variable slope, pulled downwards by weight and health, which becomes a medical deficiency only in a minority of cases. Training is therefore not judged on its ability to “raise hormones” but on what it does to muscle, bone and heart.

It remains to see what these hormonal changes do to the body. We start with bone, which is the best documented.

Step 2 of 6 · Bone

Around the final period, bone loses more in three years than in the five years before

The best measurement again comes from SWAN. The researchers followed bone density in 862 women, aged 46.7 on average at baseline, and aligned their measurements not on age but on the date of the final period. This makes it possible to see what is due to menopause and not to age.8

Bone loss is concentrated in the three years around the final period

Annual change in bone density, in percent per year, in the white women of the cohort (reference group). The values come from the tables of the article; the text sometimes gives −1.04 and −1.15 for the period after. Source: Greendale et al., J Bone Miner Res, 2012.8

What this means

Before menopause, bone is almost stable (less than 0.1% a year). Around the final period, it loses 2.5% a year at the lumbar spine and 1.8% at the femoral neck, then the rate falls back to about 1.1% a year. Over the ten years followed (5 years before, 5 years after), the cumulative loss is 10.6% at the spine and 9.1% at the femoral neck, and about 7.4% of those 10.6% occur in the three-year window around the final period alone, close to 70% of the total (derived calculation). This is not steady wear: it is a blow, concentrated in a short period, with lasting effects.

The figures are those of a reference group: loss is faster at the femoral neck in women of Chinese or Japanese origin, smaller in African-American women, and slower when body mass index is higher. The study describes density, not fractures.8

If bone loses this much in a short window, what about the rest of the body?

Step 3 of 6 · Muscle, fat and arteries

The same window changes body composition and the profile of the arteries

Still in SWAN, another team measured body composition by absorptiometry (DXA) around the final period. Before the transition, fat mass and lean mass both increase. At the start of the transition, the rate of fat gain doubles and lean mass starts to fall. These movements last until about two years after the final period, then both curves flatten.9

Total weight, for its part, does not accelerate: the sum of fat plus muscle changes at the same rate before and during the transition.9 The scale may not move while you lose muscle and gain fat, which makes it a poor indicator in this period.

Third area, the arteries. In 1,054 SWAN women, LDL (the “bad” cholesterol) rises sharply in the 12 months around the final period: the slope goes from about 1.6 mg/dL per year before, to about 5.2 in the window, then to 0.1 after. Total cholesterol follows the same shape. By contrast, systolic blood pressure rises by about 0.26 mmHg per year, a rate that follows age with no peak at the time of menopause.10

What this means

Within the same window of a few years, bone loses fast, muscle gives way to fat without the weight showing it, and the lipid profile worsens. These are averages, not you; and the curves flatten about two years after the final period, which does not mean that what was lost is recovered.

What has been lost, can it be preserved, or even regained? We start with the tool that acts most directly on bone and muscle: load.

Step 4 of 6 · Strength

Lifting heavy, in a supervised way, builds bone and strength in postmenopausal women

The most telling trial is called LIFTMOR. It randomly assigned 101 postmenopausal women, aged 65 on average, who already had low bone density. One group followed for 8 months a supervised programme of two 30-minute sessions a week: deadlift, overhead press and squat at about 80 to 85% of maximum load (5 sets of 5 repetitions), plus jumps with landing. The other group followed a light programme at home, designed for balance and mobility, with very little stimulus for bone.11

The group that lifted heavy gained bone and strength, the light group lost or nearly so

Change after 8 months, in percent, with intention-to-treat analysis. The two panels do not have the same vertical scale. 101 women aged 65 ± 5 with low bone density. Source: Watson et al., LIFTMOR, J Bone Miner Res, 2018.11

What this means

The gap at the lumbar spine is 4.1 percentage points (2.9 versus −1.2, derived calculation), and 2.2 at the femoral neck (0.3 versus −1.9). It is not just “less loss”: the bone of the spine increased. Leg extensor strength rose by 35% versus 8%, and the timed up and go test improved by 4.4% in the heavy group whereas it worsened by 1.7% in the other. In plain terms: better bone, more leg strength, and a faster everyday movement.11

The conditions matter: supervised work, 92% attendance, one minor back injury in the heavy group, no fractures, and relatively healthy participants (serious musculoskeletal or cardiovascular conditions were excluded, and the trial was not designed to measure safety).11 It shows what this work does under good conditions, not that everyone can do it alone.

One trial is not enough. What do the syntheses say?

The syntheses point in the same direction, with very unequal margins of uncertainty

Mean differences in change in bone density, in percentage points, with 95% confidence interval. An interval that crosses 0 means the effect is not established. Sources: Cochrane (Howe et al., 43 trials, 4,320 postmenopausal women) and O'Bryan et al., Sports Medicine, 2022.12,13

What this means

In the Cochrane review, 43 trials and 4,320 postmenopausal women, exercise limits bone loss. Combined programmes give about 3.2 points more at the spine than no exercise, and leg strength training about 1 point more at the femoral neck. In people aged 65 and over (14 trials), the hip gains about 2.8 points, but the spine shows no clear effect (the interval runs from −1.4 to +4.6). The authors of this latter synthesis note very high heterogeneity for bone (I² of 98.6%): the trials do not resemble one another, so the exact figure is uncertain, whereas the one for strength is more solid.12,13

Another meta-analysis of seven small studies (including 141 men) finds no significant effect on bone density, its authors stressing the small sample sizes.14 Cochrane does not find a significant difference in fractures either (7 women in 100 among those who train, 11 in 100 otherwise, a gap that may be due to chance, odds ratio 0.61, interval 0.23 to 1.64), and judges the reporting quality of the trials to be poor.12

What this means

For bone, the most solid evidence is that load, especially heavy and supervised, limits loss and can even produce gains at some sites. What is not demonstrated: that this reduces fractures. Density is a risk indicator, not the fracture itself.

What about muscle and fat, and what does cardio do?

Step 5 of 6 · Cardio, and what it leaves aside

Cardio and strength do not act on the same things

The largest synthesis on body composition after menopause pools 101 trials and 5,697 women. All exercise types combined, lean mass increases by 0.66 kg and fat mass falls by 1.27 kg; the breakdown by type is more useful.15

Strength builds muscle, cardio does not build any but burns off fat

Mean results of 101 trials, 5,697 postmenopausal women. Scale: 80 px per percentage point for fat, 120 px per kg for lean mass. The confidence interval is not reported by subgroup in the article read. Source: Khalafi et al., Frontiers in Endocrinology, 2023.15

What this means

Strength training is the only one that clearly raises lean mass (0.9 kg); cardio does not raise it significantly. All three forms lower fat, the combined one the most (2.24 points). Limits noted by the authors: different measurements, high heterogeneity, variable health. A laboratory average is not an individual promise.

For muscle, a synthesis of 27 trials (1,989 women aged 40 to 60) points the same way: exercise improves lean mass (standardised effect 0.23, small), grip strength (0.90) and knee extension strength (0.70), so more strength than volume.16

And symptoms, sleep, mood?

This is where you need to be most careful. For hot flushes, the 2014 Cochrane review (5 trials, 733 women) judges the evidence insufficient: across three trials comparing exercise with no treatment, the effect is −0.10 (interval −0.33 to +0.13), indistinguishable from zero.18 For mood, a 2025 meta-analysis (16 trials) finds that exercise reduces depressive symptoms, with a mean effect of −1.04 (−1.46 to −0.63), very large on the face of it. But the trials are very heterogeneous (I² of 93%), small, and ten have non-blinded participants, which is unavoidable with exercise: the size of the effect is not reliable, its direction is more so.17 For sleep, we read no training trial that measures it: SWAN describes the problem, not the solution.2

What this means

Training mainly makes up for what happens to the body: muscle, strength, composition. It does not replace what depends on oestrogens: no demonstrated effect on hot flushes, a probable benefit on mood without a reliable measure, and we do not know for sleep.

It remains to look at the men's side, then to put everything above to the test.

Step 6 of 6 · Men, objections, limits

In men, the evidence is thinner, and hormone treatment is not a shortcut

For men, there are fewer specific trials. The most useful is a 20-week Danish trial of 148 men aged 70 and over with mobility difficulties and low testosterone (median 8 nmol/L). Four groups: testosterone injections, strength training with calcium, vitamin D and protein, both, or nothing. On the 30-second chair stand, the combined group manages a median of 13 stands versus 10 for the control (3 more). Testosterone alone does not change this test, and training alone is not reported separately in the abstract: we cannot say what each one does.19

Two large trials shed light on what testosterone treatment does in men with low testosterone.

Testosterone improves some things a little, and did not protect bones

The two panels do not have the same scale. On the left, pooled result of the three trials, not significant in the physical function trial taken alone. On the right, risk ratio 1.43 for fractures on testosterone. Sources: Testosterone Trials, NEJM, 2016 (abstract); TRAVERSE, NEJM, 2024 (press report).20,21

What this means

In symptomatic men aged 65 and over with low testosterone, one year of gel increased sexual activity, desire and erectile function, and mood slightly, with no benefit on vitality nor, in an established way, on walking (gain of at least 50 m: 20.5% versus 12.6% in the pooled analysis, but not in the physical function trial alone).20 In TRAVERSE (men aged 40 to 80, testosterone below 300 ng/dL), there were more fractures on testosterone, 3.5% versus 2.5%, risk ratio 1.43.21 This is not an argument against a treatment decided by a doctor for a real deficiency: it is a reason not to expect it to cure the loss of muscle and bone.

Objection 1: women who train are already healthier

That holds for observational studies, not for the trials cited here, where groups are drawn by lot. But trial participants are volunteers, motivated and relatively healthy, as the LIFTMOR authors write: the results do not automatically transfer to severe osteoporosis, a history of fractures or heart disease.11

Objection 2: a gain in bone density, does that mean fewer fractures?

Not demonstrated. Cochrane finds no significant drop in fractures, and LIFTMOR was not large enough to measure them.11,12 Bone density is a good risk indicator, not a guarantee.

Objection 3: what about menopausal hormone therapy?

One sentence, without medical advice: the North American Menopause Society (NAMS, 2022 position) states that hormone therapy remains the most effective treatment for hot flushes, that it also prevents bone loss and fractures, and that its benefit-risk balance is generally favourable for healthy women under 60 and within 10 years of menopause, to be decided case by case with a doctor.22 Training and treatment are not opposed; the decision belongs to the patient and her doctor.

The answer to the problem

The question was: can training preserve muscle, bone and health when hormones fall, and what can it not preserve? Here is the answer, with its level of certainty.

Solid. In women, menopause comes with bone loss concentrated around the final period (about 70% of the ten-year loss in the three-year window, derived calculation), a decline in lean mass and a gain in fat without visible weight gain. Strength training, especially heavy and supervised, builds strength and lean mass. It limits bone loss, and even reverses it at some sites. Cardio lowers fat but does not build muscle. In men, the fall in testosterone is slow, variable, and becomes a medical deficiency only with specific symptoms.

Probable. The effects on bone are confirmed in syntheses, but with wide intervals, and the hip responds better than the spine in people over 65. A benefit on mood is probable, its size is not.

Not demonstrated. Fewer fractures thanks to training; an effect on hot flushes; an effect on sleep; the idea that training raises testosterone (in the study read, physical activity was not linked to hormonal changes); the effectiveness of testosterone on muscle and bone in men with low testosterone (TRAVERSE did not show protection of bones). In men, no trial read cleanly separates what training does alone.

The most honest summary: training does not make up for the hormones, it partly makes up for their consequences on the body, better on muscle and strength than on the rest. What it does not make up for is down to the hormone: hot flushes and, for some men, symptoms of a real deficiency. The discussion is then a medical one.

What to put in place

What follows is ordered. The training parameters are those of the trials read, not personal prescriptions. The retest frequency is an editorial choice, not a study result.

  1. Measure your strength and endurance with the tests on this page.Leg strength is the capacity the trials track closely (chair stand, knee extension, timed up and go). These field tests estimate, they do not diagnose bone or hormones: bone density is measured by a bone densitometry scan prescribed by a doctor.
  2. Put strength first, with load.The trials use progressive work on the large muscle groups (squat, deadlift, press) two to three times a week, for at least six weeks for muscle16 and several months for bone.11 The LIFTMOR trial was supervised: if you have osteoporosis, back pain or heart disease, have the programme validated by a health professional before lifting heavy.
  3. Add cardio for fat, general health and mood.Cardio does not build muscle in the syntheses read, but it lowers fat mass, and strength plus cardio together gives the biggest drop (2.24 points).15 The mood trials are mostly aerobic and mixed programmes.17
  4. Do not judge your progress by the scale.Weight does not accelerate during the transition while composition changes.9 Look at your strength, your waist measurements and your tests rather than your weight.
  5. Retest every 8 to 12 weeks, under the same conditions.Same time, same warm-up, same equipment. Below this interval, the variation between two attempts is too close to measurement noise to be interpreted.
  6. Leave medical decisions to a doctor.Troublesome menopausal symptoms, persistent fatigue, unusual drop in desire, a history of fracture: these are subjects for a consultation. A hormone test is not decided on the basis of a fitness test or an article.
What these figures do not say
  • Exercise studies measure markers (bone density, lean mass, strength) over a few months, not fractures or lifespan.
  • The SWAN cohort describes group averages; the age at the final period, ethnic origin and weight change the figures, and the bone values are those of a reference group.
  • Exercise trials last 8 months or less; few concern men with low testosterone, and the one read does not separate training from supplements. Several sources were read from the abstract only.

Frequently asked questions

Does andropause exist?

The term is contested. A gradual decline in testosterone exists, but it is slow, variable and linked to weight and health; late-onset testosterone deficiency is defined medically by at least three sexual symptoms and a measured low testosterone.4,5

Is it too late to start after 60?

The LIFTMOR participants were 65 on average with already low bone density, and they gained strength and bone in 8 months under supervision. The syntheses on people aged 65 and over point the same way for strength and the hip.11,13

Should you have your testosterone tested?

That is a matter for a doctor, based on specific symptoms. Neither this article nor a fitness test replaces that opinion.
